newsitem.title: INDIA: New India trade policy seen relaxing import controls.
newsitem.headline: New India trade policy seen relaxing import controls.

text.p: India's new five-year trade policy is likely to sweep away a battery of controls on imports and contain strong medicine to revive flagging exports, trade analysts said on Sunday.

They said the export-import policy for 1997-2002 (April-March), due on Monday, would be underpinned by India's pledge to the World Trade Organisation (WTO) to liberalise imports and New Delhi's aim of aligning import tariffs with those of other fast-growing Asian nations.
"It is expected to be a very important landmark in trade policy," trade analyst Arun Goel told Reuters.

Goel said he expected the government to remove as many as one-third of the 3,000 items on the negative list, which completely bans imports, and allow them to be imported either freely or on a case-by-case basis.
India has agreed to present the WTO in June with a time-table to phase out restrictions on imports, and analysts say the trade policy would form the blueprint of the schedule.
Commerce Minister Bolla Buli Ramaiah said on March 7 that he planned to present a "big, dynamic policy", in line with a market-oriented economic reforms programme launched in 1991.
On March 17, Finance Minister P. Chidambaram backed his claim, saying that easing curbs on consumer goods imports was an option that the government would decide on in the trade policy.
Ramu Deora, president of the Federation of Indian Export Organisations, said the policy would relax import restrictions on consumer durables in particular.
"So what if we see a sharp rise in consumer goods imports?" Deora said. "It will make smuggling less attractive while ensuring some revenue to the government (through a modest levy)."
Analyst Alok Churiwala at Bombay-based brokerage Gaurishanker Churiwala said electronics and white goods-makers were likely to feel the pinch.
"You could see a shake-out," he said. "The inefficient companies will close down. It will make Indian firms leaner and meaner."
Surging foreign exchange reserves have hardened the rupee -- which could both hurt exports and fuel rapidly rising inflation unless imports are liberalised further, the analysts said.

India's foreign exchange reserves stood at $20.68 billion on March 14 against $16.8 billion a year earlier. Inflation measured by wholesale prices was at 7.78 percent, up from 5.13 percent a year ago.

T.P. Bhat, international trade adviser at the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry of India, said India would ease curbs on imports to bolster export growth, which slowed to 6.2 percent between April 1996 and January 1997 from 22.12 percent in the same months of 1995-96.
India's trade deficit widened to $4.29 billion between April 1996 and January 1997, compared with $4.06 billion in the same period a year earlier.
Bhat said he expected import duty on capital goods, now at about 25 percent, to be slashed to five percent or less.
He said India would make exporters' norms more flexible, simplify rules for exporters' inputs and focus on agricultural products and high-technology goods exports.
